drawing_room_sw.label: Salon Art Hang
drawing_room_sw.note: Helen's private gallery — a restrained hang where quality outranks quantity, with a Freddy Hemley B&W architectural print in the formal register the Glebe demands.

drawing_room_sw.label: Limestone Fireplace
drawing_room_sw.note: West-wall fireplace with herringbone firebox, sharing a chimney stack with the Oval Dining Room next door — the natural Georgian flue line rising through the center of the house.

drawing_room_sw.label: Conservation Sash
drawing_room_sw.note: West sash with conservation IGU (UV-filtering interlayer, low-solar-gain low-E) and motorized louvered shutters on a sun-angle automation circuit — defense in depth so Helen keeps the afternoon light and the collection stays safe.

drawing_room_sw.label: South Garden View
drawing_room_sw.note: Twelve-over-twelve south sash framing the rear garden and canyon edge beyond, porch-shaded in summer — Glebe fenestration with Hill Country light.

drawing_room_sw.label: Mustard Bookshelf
drawing_room_sw.note: Captain Jack's one deliberate eccentricity within Glebe formality — a mustard-painted bookshelf, its warmth set against the room's deep red walls.

great_room_se.label: Spindrift Wall
great_room_se.note: The Spindrift principle: raw limestone and exposed timber above, white plaster below — one of the few places in the house where the stone speaks unfinished.

great_room_se.label: Bare Limestone Hearth
great_room_se.note: Limestone fireplace wall facing the front porch — the stone left undressed so Hill Country ground claims the room's visual center.

great_room_se.label: Porch-Shaded Sash
great_room_se.note: South-facing twelve-over-twelve sash under the porch overhang; a continuous clerestory above lifts light over the porch roof into the room.

great_room_se.label: Sunday Afternoon
great_room_se.note: Coffee table covered in Legos, open books, and children's drawings — Rule IV says the house is not a showroom, and this room proves it.

great_room_se.label: Blue Painted Floor
great_room_se.note: Faded grey-blue painted wood — Captain Jack's ground layer, setting the room's casual register against the Glebe's formal proportions.

library_ne.label: Bay Window Seat
library_ne.note: Canted bay on the north wall, mirrored by the Primary Suite's cantilevered cedar oriel directly above — the Glebe's paired bays reading the canyon.

library_ne.label: Canyon North View
library_ne.note: Hill Country canopy rolling to the horizon — the Library's accepted 27 FC makes this the compound's one deliberately moody room.

library_ne.label: Crammed Shelves
library_ne.note: White-painted shelves with books, pottery, photographs, and a geode interrupting the spines — genuinely used, never styled.

library_ne.label: Limestone Fireplace
library_ne.note: Limestone hearth on the south wall with the fire lit — reading lamps are load-bearing in this room because the deep wall color absorbs daylight.

library_ne.label: Deep Wall Color
library_ne.note: Deep teal-green or rich navy (Imber's call) — Captain Jack's soul claiming the ground layer in the Glebe's most bookish room.

oval_dining_nw.label: Cedar Bay Frames
oval_dining_nw.note: Helen's decision: cedar over steel, locking warmth. The grain reads natural inside; outside, it weathers to silver-grey over decades.

oval_dining_nw.label: Conical Roof
oval_dining_nw.note: Timber rafters converging to a point above the curved bay — the Glebe c.1800 addition vocabulary at its most dramatic.

oval_dining_nw.label: Limestone Window Seat
oval_dining_nw.note: Continuous stone seat running the full arc, cushioned in indigo linen — Thanksgiving guests pile in here.

oval_dining_nw.label: Dusty Pink Plaster
oval_dining_nw.note: The only color in the Main Block's public rooms — a Glebe formality that reads as warmth, not decoration.

oval_dining_nw.label: Canyon Through Cedar
oval_dining_nw.note: Five sash panels framing the north view — every season through cedar mullions, live oaks in foreground.

kitchen.label: La Cornue CornuFé
kitchen.note: CornuFé 110 in Ivory and Polished Brass — installed Phase 2A before the kitchen is even finished, because this range waits for no one.

kitchen.label: Teal Backsplash
kitchen.note: Glossy handmade teal subway tile behind the range only — Captain Jack's color note contained to one bold rectangle of wall.

kitchen.label: Copper Hood
kitchen.note: Broad darkened copper greening at the edges — Hill Country craft tradition meeting Provincetown patina; it looks better every year.

kitchen.label: Cobalt Island
kitchen.note: Deep cobalt blue polished concrete with Hill Country limestone aggregate visible in the surface — the kitchen's soul in one slab.

kitchen.label: Herb Terrace Doors
kitchen.note: South-wall French doors to the herb terrace — rosemary and thyme three steps from the cutting board, live oaks framing the view.

entry_hall_front_s_ctr.label: Heated Limestone Floor
entry_hall_front_s_ctr.note: Honed limestone flags with geothermal radiant heat in the slab — warm underfoot on January mornings, the Hill Country ground you walk in on.

entry_hall_front_s_ctr.label: Octagonal Grand Stair
entry_hall_front_s_ctr.note: Open-well stair wrapping a faceted perimeter with turned cedar balusters and walnut handrail — oculus light falls the full double height.

entry_hall_front_s_ctr.label: Stair Wall Photos
entry_hall_front_s_ctr.note: Crowded mismatched frames climbing the wall — the compound's visual autobiography, started on move-in day and never finished.

entry_hall_front_s_ctr.label: Dome to Oculus
entry_hall_front_s_ctr.note: Helen's pick: sealed dome-to-oculus crown with a 6-foot glass pane — the falling light is the Entry Hall's soul moment.

entry_hall_front_s_ctr.label: Woven Rag Rug
entry_hall_front_s_ctr.note: Captain Jack's on top of the Glebe's most formal material — color and wear on stone, because someone lives here.

primary_bedroom_ne_over_library.label: Vertical Beadboard
primary_bedroom_ne_over_library.note: White beadboard feature wall — Captain Jack's signature transplanted from the harbor, with Glebe proportions holding the room's Georgian bones.

primary_bedroom_ne_over_library.label: Bedroom Gallery
primary_bedroom_ne_over_library.note: Mismatched landscapes and portraits on beadboard — the bedroom wall is personal and private, not curated for visitors.

primary_bedroom_ne_over_library.label: Canyon Bluffs
primary_bedroom_ne_over_library.note: French doors to the Primary Terrace — the canyon's limestone bluffs visible from bed, morning coffee in bare feet.

primary_bedroom_ne_over_library.label: Exposed Roof Timber
primary_bedroom_ne_over_library.note: Honest ceiling structure — Rule III says no coffered ceilings, no tray ceilings, no faux beams; what's there is what you see.

primary_bedroom_ne_over_library.label: Morning East Light
primary_bedroom_ne_over_library.note: Three east sash windows bringing morning light into the bedroom — the sunrise wall warms the room before the canyon does.

sunroom.label: Steel Pivot Panels
sunroom.note: Black steel panels fold completely open — the boundary between inside and pool terrace dissolves to a single continuous limestone plane.

sunroom.label: Pool and Canyon
sunroom.note: Zero-entry pool in foreground, Hill Country canyon dropping away behind — the Wharf Wing's defining view through open steel.

sunroom.label: Continuous Limestone
sunroom.note: Honed limestone running without a break from inside to pool deck — no threshold, no transition, the ground is one surface.

sunroom.label: Rattan and Stripe
sunroom.note: Rattan sofa with blue-white striped cushions — Captain Jack's casual permanence transplanted from the harbor to the canyon edge.

sunroom.label: Limestone Party Wall
sunroom.note: Raw limestone from the Main Block — the Sunroom reads the house's stone body from inside the cedar-shingled Wharf Wing.

everyday_dining_n_ctr.label: Golden Ochre Walls
everyday_dining_n_ctr.note: Captain Jack's warmest color — the room the family eats in every day, from move-in morning through every decade after.

everyday_dining_n_ctr.label: Pine Farmhouse Table
everyday_dining_n_ctr.note: Scrubbed pine with mismatched chairs — breakfast mess, homework, crayon marks that no one cleans up because they're the point.

everyday_dining_n_ctr.label: Victorian Chest
everyday_dining_n_ctr.note: Worn white chest with photographs on top — the room's memory shelf, never dusted and never styled.

everyday_dining_n_ctr.label: Orangery Doors
everyday_dining_n_ctr.note: Three French doors plus continuous transom opening north to the Orangery — morning coffee becomes a garden experience.

guest_sitting.label: Beadboard to Roofline
guest_sitting.note: White vertical beadboard running full height — full Captain Jack's, no limestone, no Glebe formality, no compromise.

guest_sitting.label: Provincetown Salon
guest_sitting.note: Sailboats, harbor scenes, watercolors in mismatched frames — Provincetown's visual vocabulary covering the wall the way it does on the Wharf.

guest_sitting.label: Vaulted Cedar
guest_sitting.note: Dark timber rafters over beadboard — honest structure exposed because Rule III demands it, and the harbor always showed its bones.

guest_sitting.label: Grey Painted Floor
guest_sitting.note: Grey painted wood throughout the Guest Suite — quiet enough to let the art talk, worn enough to feel like it's always been here.

guest_sitting.label: Pool Through Sash
guest_sitting.note: Tall sash windows onto the pool terrace — Captain Jack's harbor water reinterpreted as Texas waterside.

guest_bedroom.label: Iron Bed Frame
guest_bedroom.note: White iron bed with plaid throw and navy pillows — mismatched and inherited, nothing that reads as purchased together.

guest_bedroom.label: Pool at the Door
guest_bedroom.note: French doors opening directly onto the pool deck — the morning swim is three steps from the pillow.

guest_bedroom.label: Freddy's Provincetown
guest_bedroom.note: Two or three Freddy Hemley photographs — harbor and waterfront, the Forum 49 connection felt most clearly in this room.

guest_bedroom.label: Red Painted Dresser
guest_bedroom.note: Captain Jack's mismatched furniture rule: nothing matching, everything loved, every piece telling a different story.

guest_en_suite.label: Corner Clawfoot Tub
guest_en_suite.note: Porcelain tub with shell-foot detail — behind it, a 36×48 barrier-free shower rough-in waits for future aging-in-place.

guest_en_suite.label: Beadboard Wainscot
guest_en_suite.note: Continuous with the sitting room and bedroom — the Guest Suite's vocabulary doesn't stop at the bathroom door.

guest_en_suite.label: Verdigris Faucet
guest_en_suite.note: Salvage-look brass with natural patina — Captain Jack's insists hardware looks like it's been there for decades.

guest_en_suite.label: Live Oak Through Sash
guest_en_suite.note: Dark-framed sash window with a live oak filling the view — a bath with a tree in it.

right_passage_freddy_s_gallery.label: Main Block Limestone
right_passage_freddy_s_gallery.note: The Main Block's stone face visible through the glass — Freddy's photographs hang on the solid walls, Haiti on one side, New England on the other.

right_passage_freddy_s_gallery.label: Glass Between Worlds
right_passage_freddy_s_gallery.note: Floor-to-ceiling glass joining limestone Main Block to cedar-shingled Wharf Wing — the compound's two materials face each other across this passage.

right_passage_freddy_s_gallery.label: Pool and Canyon
right_passage_freddy_s_gallery.note: Every walk from the Great Room to the pool passes through Freddy's work with the canyon view beside it.

right_passage_freddy_s_gallery.label: Picture Light
right_passage_freddy_s_gallery.note: Gallery-grade wall-wash lighting in a passage — climate-controlled, museum-standard display for the collection's most public location.

upper_gallery_landing.label: Salon Hang
upper_gallery_landing.note: Paintings, photographs, children's art mixed at different heights — the hang the family adds to for decades, never declared finished.

upper_gallery_landing.label: North Sash / Writing Desk
upper_gallery_landing.note: Tall sash at the north end with Hill Country view — a small writing desk sits here for letters and looking.

upper_gallery_landing.label: Walnut Handrail
upper_gallery_landing.note: Walnut rail and white-painted balusters from the Georgian stair vocabulary — the Glebe's bones continued from the Entry Hall below.

upper_gallery_landing.label: Windowsill Life
upper_gallery_landing.note: Photos propped on the sill, books stacked, candle left from last night — the gallery is a room in its own right, not a hallway.

upper_gallery_landing.label: Falling Oculus Light
upper_gallery_landing.note: Light from the dome-to-oculus descends through the open stair well — this is where you look up and see it land two floors below.

orangery.label: Swing Daybed
orangery.note: Rope-hung daybed with striped cushions — children's nap space, sunset-watching perch, the room's most Captain Jack's gesture.

orangery.label: Canyon Sunset
orangery.note: Glass walls facing the canyon — the Orangery is where sunset becomes architecture, not just a view.

orangery.label: Main Block Stone Face
orangery.note: Raw limestone of the north elevation visible inside the Orangery — reading the house's body from outside its body.

orangery.label: Rattan Dining
orangery.note: Wine, bread, rattan chairs — the informal supper that makes the Oval Dining Room's formality mean something by contrast.

study_sw_over_drawing.label: Working Shelves
study_sw_over_drawing.note: Floor-to-ceiling on both sides — the Study mirrors the Library below but belongs to Jon's working mind, not the family's browsing.

study_sw_over_drawing.label: Live Oak View
study_sw_over_drawing.note: Bay window framing live oaks and Hill Country — the view Jon works in front of every day, deliberately not a screen.

study_sw_over_drawing.label: Limestone Hearth
study_sw_over_drawing.note: Limestone fireplace flanking the shelves — Hill Country ground layer anchoring the Glebe proportions in a room built for thinking.

study_sw_over_drawing.label: Desk Surface
study_sw_over_drawing.note: Open books, coffee, a pen — the desk is the room's purpose; everything else exists to make this surface productive.

study_sw_over_drawing.label: Window Seat
study_sw_over_drawing.note: Blue-striped cushion with books piled at one end — the reading position that isn't the desk, for when thinking needs to change posture.

quiet_room_s_ctr.label: Picture Window
quiet_room_s_ctr.note: Single uninterrupted pane — the accepted deviation from twelve-over-twelve, because muntins in this contemplative room would read as fussy.

quiet_room_s_ctr.label: Cedar Window Seat
quiet_room_s_ctr.note: Built-in seat framing the Hill Country panorama — the room's primary position for looking without doing.

quiet_room_s_ctr.label: Limestone Fireplace
quiet_room_s_ctr.note: Fireplace on the west wall with books and landscape painting on the mantel — Hill Country ground anchoring the room's stillness.

quiet_room_s_ctr.label: Honey Clerestory
quiet_room_s_ctr.note: Antique-cast honey glass facing the stair hall — borrowed warm light from the fanlight below, soul not lux, the compound's only tinted glazing.

quiet_room_s_ctr.label: Reading Chair
quiet_room_s_ctr.note: Leather wingback with brass lamp — entered through a concealed jib door from the Study, this room hides from the rest of the house.

front_porch.label: Front Door
front_porch.note: Mesquite and cedar with iron hardware in a Glebe stone surround — semi-circular fanlight with radiating muntins and flanking sidelights, matte finish.

front_porch.label: Dark Green Shutters
front_porch.note: Helen-locked: operable dark green painted shutters on all sash windows, with motorized conduit rough-in for conservation and storm automation.

front_porch.label: Tuscan Columns
front_porch.note: Classical Tuscan order supporting the twelve-foot porch — Glebe bones at Texas scale, proportioned by Imber.

front_porch.label: Fanlight
front_porch.note: UV-filtering Low-E glazing in the semi-circular transom — south light enters here and rises through the Entry Hall to the Quiet Room honey clerestory above.

front_porch.label: Stone Veneer
front_porch.note: Locally quarried limestone on a ventilated rainscreen with six-inch-deep window returns — the visual weight of solid masonry from skilled construction.

powder_room.label: Dark Jewel-Box Walls
powder_room.note: Saturated Captain Jack's color — a deliberate light-to-dark counterpoint encountered off the bright octagonal stair hall.

powder_room.label: Salon Hang
powder_room.note: Children's watercolors and family art covering the dark wall — the windowless room is conservation-ideal for light-sensitive pieces.

powder_room.label: Brass and Stone
powder_room.note: Wall-mounted basin with brass cross-handle faucets against limestone side walls — Glebe material meeting Captain Jack's hardware.

powder_room.label: Storm Shelter Door
powder_room.note: Shelter #2: reinforced but deliberately residential-looking door panelized to match millwork — operable by one person in seconds, PoE/Wi-Fi inside.

aurelia_s_provincetown_suite_nw_over_ova.label: Stacked Curved Oriel
aurelia_s_provincetown_suite_nw_over_ova.note: Five sash panels mirroring the Oval Dining bay directly below — the Glebe's paired vertical rhythm, canyon panorama from Aurelia's bed.

aurelia_s_provincetown_suite_nw_over_ova.label: Collage Wall
aurelia_s_provincetown_suite_nw_over_ova.note: Photos, postcards, ticket stubs pinned and taped — the one wall in the house designed to be covered by a teenager, not an architect.

aurelia_s_provincetown_suite_nw_over_ova.label: Turntable
aurelia_s_provincetown_suite_nw_over_ova.note: Every major living space gets a turntable position — in Aurelia's room it sits center-stage in the bay, music facing the canyon.

aurelia_s_provincetown_suite_nw_over_ova.label: Green Velvet Sofa
aurelia_s_provincetown_suite_nw_over_ova.note: Curved sofa with stuffed animals — Captain Jack's accumulated-life quality operating as a teenager's actual living room.

aurelia_s_provincetown_suite_nw_over_ova.label: Cedar Ceiling
aurelia_s_provincetown_suite_nw_over_ova.note: Exposed timber structure — the ceiling above the Oval Dining's conical roof becomes the room's overhead character.

rafa_s_texas_room_se_over_great.label: Limestone Headboard Wall
rafa_s_texas_room_se_over_great.note: Raw stone as the bed's backdrop — Hill Country ground claiming the room's primary ancestor; the cowboy hat confirms the territory.

rafa_s_texas_room_se_over_great.label: East Sash Windows
rafa_s_texas_room_se_over_great.note: Tall south and east sash flooding the room with morning light — this room sits directly above the Great Room.

rafa_s_texas_room_se_over_great.label: Window Bookcase
rafa_s_texas_room_se_over_great.note: Olive green low bookcase running the window wall — books, colored pencils, treasures at a child's height.

rafa_s_texas_room_se_over_great.label: Kilim Quilt
rafa_s_texas_room_se_over_great.note: Southwest textile on a cedar bed frame — Hill Country ground layer in the fabric, not just the stone.

primary_en_suite_teal.label: Freestanding Tub
primary_en_suite_teal.note: Soaking tub centered under the arched window — the room's anchor, brass faucet on axis with the view above.

primary_en_suite_teal.label: Sea Glass Mosaic
primary_en_suite_teal.note: Teal and aqua pebble detail in the window recess — Captain Jack's harbor memory rendered in bathroom material.

primary_en_suite_teal.label: Beadboard Walls
primary_en_suite_teal.note: White vertical beadboard continuous with the Primary Bedroom — the suite reads as one vocabulary across bed, bath, and dressing.

primary_en_suite_teal.label: Glass Shower
primary_en_suite_teal.note: Natural stone tile with brass hardware — grab-bar blocking behind tile at all wet locations for aging-in-place.

pink_en_suite_aurelia.label: Pink Herringbone Shower
pink_en_suite_aurelia.note: Arched niche with pink chevron tile — Aurelia's color carried from the Oval Dining's dusty pink into her private bathroom.

pink_en_suite_aurelia.label: Brass Rain Shower
pink_en_suite_aurelia.note: Exposed brass fixtures aging naturally — unlacquered brass is compound-wide, and it looks better every year.

pink_en_suite_aurelia.label: Penny Tile Floor
pink_en_suite_aurelia.note: Warm copper penny rounds — the floor's color rhymes with the shower tile without matching it.

pink_en_suite_aurelia.label: Seascape Painting
pink_en_suite_aurelia.note: A small harbor painting above the tub — Captain Jack's soul in the children's bathroom, not just the public rooms.

rafa_en_suite.label: Pedestal Tub
rafa_en_suite.note: Freestanding tub with brass wall-mount faucet — scaled for a child's bathroom, grown-up enough to last.

rafa_en_suite.label: Beadboard Wainscot
rafa_en_suite.note: Vertical beadboard below a warm peach upper wall — Hill Country warmth meeting Captain Jack's board vocabulary.

rafa_en_suite.label: Live Oak Window
rafa_en_suite.note: Corner sash with family photos propped on the sill — the view is a tree, not a landscape, and that's enough.

rafa_en_suite.label: Bath Toy Basket
rafa_en_suite.note: Woven basket full of toys next to a red step stool — Rule IV says the house is lived in, including the bathroom.

primary_dressing.label: Center Island
primary_dressing.note: White cabinetry island with brass-edged counter and leather storage below — the dressing room organized around a working surface.

primary_dressing.label: Brass Picture Light
primary_dressing.note: Gold-framed mirror under a brass picture light — the room's one deliberate moment of vanity in a house that resists it.

primary_dressing.label: Open Shelving
primary_dressing.note: Cedar shelves on white beadboard — visible storage, not hidden; the dressing room reads as a room, not a closet.

primary_dressing.label: Brass Hardware
primary_dressing.note: Unlacquered brass pulls compound-wide — the dressing room uses the same hardware language as the Kitchen and Entry Hall.

primary_terrace.label: Canyon Panorama
primary_terrace.note: The compound's deepest private view — limestone bluffs and Hill Country canopy extending to the horizon from the upper floor.

primary_terrace.label: Weathered Chairs
primary_terrace.note: Teak armchairs with blue-striped cushions aging in the sun — Captain Jack's harbor furniture living outdoors.

primary_terrace.label: Painted Metal Table
primary_terrace.note: Distressed drum table with coffee and lemons — the terrace furniture is not precious, it's used every morning.

primary_terrace.label: Bedroom Threshold
primary_terrace.note: French doors to the Primary Suite — zero-threshold transition for aging-in-place, canyon air into the room.

covered_walkway.label: Limestone Columns
covered_walkway.note: Square piers joining the Main Block to the Service Wing — the Covered Walkway is a limestone loggia, not a corridor.

covered_walkway.label: Cedar Roof Structure
covered_walkway.note: Exposed timber rafters — Hill Country utilitarian structure overhead, honest and warm.

covered_walkway.label: Limestone Flag Floor
covered_walkway.note: Zero-threshold transition at both ends — the loggia connects without interrupting the ground plane.

covered_walkway.label: Potted Herbs
covered_walkway.note: Rosemary and lavender along the Main Block wall — the Service Wing's dirty-to-clean spine begins at the landscape.

glass_bridge.label: Art on Limestone
glass_bridge.note: Framed landscapes hung on the Main Block's stone face — the bridge doubles as a gallery wall where you pass Freddy's work daily.

glass_bridge.label: Glass to Live Oaks
glass_bridge.note: Floor-to-ceiling glass on the open side — the bridge is transparent to the landscape; you walk through the canopy, not past it.

glass_bridge.label: Cedar and Glass Roof
glass_bridge.note: Timber beams with glazed panels between — the roof lets sky in overhead while the cedar matches the compound's honest-structure rule.

glass_bridge.label: Wharf Wing Shingle
glass_bridge.note: White-painted cedar shingle visible at the far end — the bridge connects limestone to shingle, and you see both materials the whole way.

glass_bridge.label: Flush Limestone Floor
glass_bridge.note: Zero-threshold transition — the same honed stone runs from the Main Block through the bridge into the Wharf Wing without a single lip or step.

pantry_wine_room.label: Stone Arch Entry
pantry_wine_room.note: Limestone arch framing the wine storage — the Fortified Wine Room doubles as Storm Shelter #1 (ICF walls, vault door, PoE/Wi-Fi inside).

pantry_wine_room.label: Wine Grid
pantry_wine_room.note: Cedar wine rack against a blue-painted back wall — Hill Country utilitarian storage with a Captain Jack's color note.

pantry_wine_room.label: Tasting Table
pantry_wine_room.note: Simple walnut table with a stool — wine from the North Alley Champanel vines and the Orangery Trebbiano ends up here.

pantry_wine_room.label: Saltillo Floor
pantry_wine_room.note: Terra cotta tile — the Service Wing's utilitarian ground layer, warm underfoot and forgiving of spills.

scullery.label: Teal Tile Alcove
scullery.note: Deep utility sink in a teal-tiled recess with brass wall-mount faucet — the decontamination buffer between outside and kitchen.

scullery.label: Tall Sash Window
scullery.note: Narrow sash bringing Hill Country light deep into the Service Wing — the workaday rooms still get a view.

scullery.label: Louvered Cabinets
scullery.note: White louvered doors with brass hardware — ventilated storage for the scullery's role as the kitchen's support spine.

scullery.label: Belfast Sink
scullery.note: Farmhouse sink with brass faucet — the scullery is where real work happens, and the sink is built for it.

mudroom.label: Blue-Green Beadboard
mudroom.note: Grey-blue-green vertical beadboard cubbies with iron hooks — the Mudroom's own color within the Provincetown board vocabulary.

mudroom.label: Cedar Bench
mudroom.note: Walnut bench with boot storage below — the dirty-to-clean spine starts here, eyes on the drive through the door.

mudroom.label: Copper Dog Wash
mudroom.note: Full-size copper tub against limestone — for the dogs after the land, before the house.

mudroom.label: Drive View Door
mudroom.note: French doors facing the approach — 'eyes on drive' so you see who's coming before they knock.

tea_station.label: Helen's Cup Collection
tea_station.note: Two shelves of mismatched colorful cups on blue-painted shelves — every mug a different trip, a different gift, a different morning.

tea_station.label: Brass Kettle
tea_station.note: Kettle and faucet at the Main Block end — the first thing reached from the house without entering the Service Wing.

tea_station.label: Tea Caddy
tea_station.note: Wooden grinder box on the counter — the station operates independently of the kitchen, always ready.

tea_station.label: Brass Hardware
tea_station.note: White cabinets with unlacquered brass knobs — the Tea Station speaks the same hardware language as the Kitchen next door.

mechanical_laundry.label: Teal Utility Alcove
mechanical_laundry.note: Tiled alcove with brass wall-mount faucet and cedar shelves — the laundry room gets the same material care as the kitchen.

mechanical_laundry.label: Sash Window
mechanical_laundry.note: Tall narrow sash bringing Hill Country light into the back of the Service Wing — even the mechanical spaces see the sky.

mechanical_laundry.label: Belfast Sink
mechanical_laundry.note: Deep farmhouse sink for hand-washing and heavy-duty cleanup — the laundry chute from the Upper Gallery empties near here.

mechanical_laundry.label: Louvered Storage
mechanical_laundry.note: Ventilated cabinets for linens and cleaning supplies — well filtration and greywater terminus equipment lives behind the finished face.

pool.label: Zero-Entry Slope
pool.note: Gentle slope facing the Sunroom — the pool begins as wet limestone before it becomes water, no edge to step over.

pool.label: Canyon Horizon
pool.note: The infinity edge faces the canyon — the water drops into the landscape and the landscape drops into the sky.

pool.label: Lunar Tidal Algorithm
pool.note: PLC-controlled 28-day cycle in the overflow coping — the pool is a Georgian Enlightenment instrument, not a utility.

pool.label: Continuous Limestone
pool.note: Honed stone running from Sunroom interior through the zero-entry to the pool surround — one surface, no break.

pool_terrace.label: Rattan Loungers
pool_terrace.note: Wicker chaises with blue-striped cushions — Captain Jack's harbor furniture arranged around the pool, not a resort.

pool_terrace.label: Reflecting Pool
pool_terrace.note: Still water mirroring the live oak canopy and the Sunroom's glass wall — the terrace is designed around this reflection.

pool_terrace.label: Sunroom Glass Wall
pool_terrace.note: The steel pivot panels visible from outside — when open, the Sunroom and terrace are one continuous space.

pool_terrace.label: Live Oak Canopy
pool_terrace.note: A single live oak framing the canyon view — the tree was here first, and the compound was placed around it.

pool_bath.label: Brass Rain Shower
pool_bath.note: Exposed brass shower fixture against white beadboard — poolside rinse-off in Captain Jack's vocabulary, not resort tile.

pool_bath.label: Beadboard Walls
pool_bath.note: White vertical beadboard continuous with the Wharf Wing — the Pool Bath speaks the same language as the Guest Suite and Sunroom.

pool_bath.label: Cedar Bench
pool_bath.note: Teak bench for changing — simple, poolside, built to get wet.

pool_bath.label: Brass Towel Hooks
pool_bath.note: A row of brass hooks with a colorful towel — the pool bath is the threshold between wet and dry.

sauna.label: Cedar Interior
sauna.note: All-cedar walls, ceiling, and floor — the sauna is pure Hill Country material, no stone, no plaster, just wood and heat.

sauna.label: Canyon Bluff Window
sauna.note: Picture window facing the limestone bluffs — you sit in heat and look at the geology that made the land.

sauna.label: Cedar Bench
sauna.note: The Wharf Wing's third climate pole: Sunroom is warm, pool is cold, sauna is hot — the full thermal range of harbor life.

cedar_pavilion.label: Timber Frame
cedar_pavilion.note: Cedar post-and-beam structure on limestone pier bases — Hill Country barn vernacular, no walls, all sky.

cedar_pavilion.label: Standing-Seam Roof
cedar_pavilion.note: Dark-bronze Galvalume matching the compound roofline — the Pavilion reads as part of the family even from the road.

cedar_pavilion.label: EV Daily Port
cedar_pavilion.note: V2G pre-wired charging location — the Pavilion is the compound's daily vehicle parking, not the Motor Barn.

cedar_pavilion.label: Firewood Cart
cedar_pavilion.note: Wheelbarrow and split wood — the working landscape starts at the edge of where you park.

north_alley_pergola.label: Corten Crossbars
north_alley_pergola.note: Corten steel disappearing under vine on limestone column bases — the metal rusts to match the land, then the grapes hide it entirely.

north_alley_pergola.label: Champanel Grapevines
north_alley_pergola.note: PD-resistant Phase 1 production grape — supersedes Black Spanish; the pergola is infrastructure, not ornament.

north_alley_pergola.label: Canyon Through Vine
north_alley_pergola.note: Hill Country rolling to the horizon framed by grape leaf and limestone — the North Alley's defining axis view.

north_alley_pergola.label: Italian Herb Beds
north_alley_pergola.note: Herbs at the column bases — the pergola's ground layer is edible, Firewise-compliant, and feeds the kitchen.

dome_oculus.label: Glass Dome
dome_oculus.note: Sealed six-foot oculus — Helen's pick; nothing passes through in or out, answering the falling-scorpion concern by spec.

dome_oculus.label: Brass Lantern
dome_oculus.note: Georgian lantern pendant hanging in the open well — the light fixture the oculus illuminates from above.

dome_oculus.label: Octagonal Stair
dome_oculus.note: Open-well stair wrapping the faceted perimeter — the elongated octagon deliberately rhyming with the Oval Dining below.

dome_oculus.label: Salon Hang
dome_oculus.note: Art and frames covering every available wall from ground to gallery — the stair hall is the compound's vertical autobiography.

dome_oculus.label: Dark-Sky Light Seal
dome_oculus.note: Motorized damper seals the thermal chimney whenever the well is lit at night — the lantern cannot leak uplight, independent of Observatory Mode.

cornelia_s_greenhouse.label: Arched Glass Wall
cornelia_s_greenhouse.note: Steel-muntin arched window looking onto live oaks — the Greenhouse's one grand gesture, light pouring onto the potting bench.

cornelia_s_greenhouse.label: Terra Cotta Shelves
cornelia_s_greenhouse.note: Cedar shelving with clay pots and seedlings — Mississippi ancestor exclusively: the tradition of growing things in utilitarian spaces.

cornelia_s_greenhouse.label: Straw Hat and Vine
cornelia_s_greenhouse.note: Trailing plant, garden hat, woven baskets — Grandma Cornelia's memorial is a working greenhouse, not a shrine.

cornelia_s_greenhouse.label: Limestone Flag Floor
cornelia_s_greenhouse.note: Irregular flagstone continuous with the Motor Barn — the Greenhouse is attached to the barn, not the house.

vehicle_bay_1.label: Arched Bays
vehicle_bay_1.note: Limestone arches opening onto the drive — Georgian proportions scaled to trucks, not carriages.

vehicle_bay_1.label: EV Charger
vehicle_bay_1.note: Wall-mounted charger between bays — V2G pre-wired Phase 2A, the compound's energy system starts at the vehicle.

vehicle_bay_1.label: Barrel-Vault Ceiling
vehicle_bay_1.note: Cedar barrel vault — the Motor Barn's interior reads as architecture, not garage.

vehicle_bay_1.label: Walnut Workbench
vehicle_bay_1.note: Coffee cup, radio, leather tool roll — the bay is a workshop that happens to store vehicles.

vehicle_bay_1.label: Storm Shelter Access
vehicle_bay_1.note: Flush-mount pit beneath the slab — Shelter #3, prefab steel, brass hinged door, PoE/Wi-Fi via buried conduit.

energy_forge.label: Battery Bank
energy_forge.note: Seven FranklinWH aPower 2 units totaling 105 kWh — sodium-ion preferred, LFP fallback; Phase 2A shell, Phase 2C install.

energy_forge.label: Monitoring Desk
energy_forge.note: Workbench with the aGate controller and SPAN panel — the compound's energy nervous system managed from one surface.

energy_forge.label: Cedar Joists
energy_forge.note: Exposed roof structure — even the battery room gets Hill Country utilitarian honesty overhead.

energy_forge.label: Limestone Wall
energy_forge.note: Raw stone on the Motor Barn's exterior face — the Energy Forge sits inside the same limestone shell as the vehicle bays.

loft.label: Dark Timber Trusses
loft.note: Exposed roof structure in the Motor Barn's vaulted loft — Hill Country barn grammar, the ceiling is the building.

loft.label: Limestone Chimney
loft.note: Raw stone chimney wall dividing the loft — the Motor Barn's structural spine doubling as the room's visual anchor.

loft.label: Air Hockey Table
loft.note: Helen's heirloom (first date) — the table stays, something else moves if there's a conflict. Non-negotiable.

loft.label: Sectional Sofa
loft.note: Olive green deep sectional with board games — the Loft is the family's second living room, less curated than the Great Room.

loft.label: Phase 2C Contingency
loft.note: First on the kill order if budget tightens — if killed, the air hockey table relocates to the Drawing Room and gets pride of place.

podcast_studio.label: Acoustic Panels
podcast_studio.note: Corner-mounted absorbers flanking a bookshelf — the booth is acoustically isolated from the loft family room on the other side of the wall.

podcast_studio.label: Condenser Mic
podcast_studio.note: Jonathan-locked space — voice acting booth and podcast studio, the room's purpose visible in one piece of equipment.

podcast_studio.label: Leather Club Chairs
podcast_studio.note: Two chairs facing each other with a low table — interview format, not broadcasting desk; the room is for conversation.

podcast_studio.label: Heavy Acoustic Door
podcast_studio.note: The threshold between the loft's family noise and the studio's silence — one door changes the compound's register entirely.

airlock.label: Limestone Arch
airlock.note: Stone surround at the thermal boundary — the arch announces that you're passing from unconditioned bays into the conditioned Motor Barn.

airlock.label: Brass Pendant
airlock.note: Conical brass light marking the transition — the airlock gets one deliberate design gesture in an otherwise utilitarian passage.

airlock.label: Brass Boot Tray
airlock.note: Floor-level tray at the threshold — gravel and mud stop here; the clean side of the Motor Barn begins on the other side.

airlock.label: Cedar Doors
airlock.note: Solid cedar doors flanking the passage — the airlock is a room, not a hallway, with doors that close on both sides.

compute_room.label: Server Racks
compute_room.note: Liquid-cooled compute hardware — waste heat feeds domestic hot water and pool through an automated switching valve.

compute_room.label: Workstation
compute_room.note: Monitor, stool, coffee cup — the Compute Room is managed on-site, not just remotely; someone sits here.

compute_room.label: Limestone Slit Window
compute_room.note: Narrow opening in the stone wall casting a blade of Hill Country light across the servers — even infrastructure sees the land.

compute_room.label: Exposed Cable Runs
compute_room.note: Cables visible overhead — Hill Country utilitarian honesty; the Compute Room doesn't pretend to be anything but what it is.

research_room.label: Walnut Research Table
research_room.note: Papers, notebooks, and coffee spread across walnut — Hill Country body with Enlightenment touches; the table is the room's purpose.

research_room.label: Mullioned Glass Doors
research_room.note: Cedar-framed French doors looking through to the Compute Room — the research instrument visible from the research space.

research_room.label: Limestone Walls
research_room.note: Raw stone on both sides — the Research Room sits inside the Motor Barn's shell, not a finished-out office.

research_room.label: Reference Library
research_room.note: Dark bookshelf with binders and files — the physical knowledge base that the Compute Room's digital one complements.

instrument_bay_upgrade.label: Empty Shell
instrument_bay_upgrade.note: Deliberately unfinished — the Instrument Bay is built as a blank room with infrastructure rough-in, waiting for equipment that doesn't exist yet.

instrument_bay_upgrade.label: Timber Ceiling
instrument_bay_upgrade.note: Cedar structure overhead — even the shell reads as Hill Country utilitarian, not warehouse.

instrument_bay_upgrade.label: Equipment Door
instrument_bay_upgrade.note: Oversized opening for moving large instruments in and out — the room is designed to accept whatever the research program needs.

instrument_bay_upgrade.label: Infrastructure Rough-In
instrument_bay_upgrade.note: Power outlets, data conduit, and climate control stubs — the bay is useless without equipment, but ready for anything with it.

observatory_tower.label: Isolated Pier
observatory_tower.note: Concrete pier poured Phase 2A during foundation work — structurally independent of the tower walls, vibration-free for the telescope mount.

observatory_tower.label: Observatory Dome
observatory_tower.note: Shell and telescope deferred Phase 2C — the pier is the only part that must go in during foundations.

observatory_tower.label: Limestone Tower Walls
observatory_tower.note: Raw limestone with multiple sash windows — the Observatory reads as a Glebe folly from outside, an instrument room from inside.

observatory_tower.label: Reading Corner
observatory_tower.note: Leather chair and bookshelf between the windows — the room doubles as a retreat when the telescope isn't in use.

observatory_tower.label: Setback Validation
observatory_tower.note: At least 200 feet from Pool, 150 feet from Motor Barn — locked distances enforced by the compound model's validation gates.

vehicle_bay_2.label: Arched Bays
vehicle_bay_2.note: Limestone arches opening onto the drive — Georgian proportions scaled to trucks, not carriages.

vehicle_bay_2.label: EV Charger
vehicle_bay_2.note: Wall-mounted charger between bays — V2G pre-wired Phase 2A, the compound's energy system starts at the vehicle.

vehicle_bay_2.label: Barrel-Vault Ceiling
vehicle_bay_2.note: Cedar barrel vault — the Motor Barn's interior reads as architecture, not garage.

vehicle_bay_2.label: Walnut Workbench
vehicle_bay_2.note: Coffee cup, radio, leather tool roll — the bay is a workshop that happens to store vehicles.

vehicle_bay_2.label: Storm Shelter Access
vehicle_bay_2.note: Flush-mount pit beneath the slab — Shelter #3, prefab steel, brass hinged door, PoE/Wi-Fi via buried conduit.

vehicle_bay_3.note: Limestone arches opening onto the drive — Georgian proportions scaled to trucks, not carriages.

vehicle_bay_3.label: EV Charger
vehicle_bay_3.note: Wall-mounted charger between bays — V2G pre-wired Phase 2A, the compound's energy system starts at the vehicle.

vehicle_bay_3.note: Cedar barrel vault — the Motor Barn's interior reads as architecture, not garage.

vehicle_bay_3.note: Coffee cup, radio, leather tool roll — the bay is a workshop that happens to store vehicles.

vehicle_bay_3.note: Flush-mount pit beneath the slab — Shelter #3, prefab steel, brass hinged door, PoE/Wi-Fi via buried conduit.
